dublinCore.description: A spectrum analyzer built on a radix-2 FFT. Generated test signals or the microphone are analyzed frame by frame with a selectable FFT size and window function, and shown as a linear magnitude, dB or phase spectrum with peak markers, a cursor readout and an optional scrolling spectrogram.

learningObjectives: Compute the bin spacing and frame length of an FFT from the sampling rate and the FFT size
Use the relation |X[k]| = A N / 2 to read the amplitude of a tone from an FFT
Compare the leakage of rectangular, Hamming, Hanning, Blackman and Kaiser windows
Explain the trade-off between frequency resolution and time resolution when the FFT size changes
Interpret a spectrogram of a steady tone, a frequency sweep and live sound

misconceptions.misconception: The height of an FFT peak is the amplitude of the tone without any scaling
misconceptions.correction: A bin-centred sine of amplitude A gives |X[k]| = A N / 2 with a rectangular window; the display divides by N/2 and the window's mean
misconceptions.evidence: For a unit sine at 1000 Hz the readout shows |X[k]| = 512 at N = 1024 and 2048 at N = 4096, while the amplitude reads 1.000 in both cases

misconceptions.misconception: Leakage is an error in the FFT algorithm
misconceptions.correction: Leakage comes from analysing a frame that does not hold a whole number of cycles; windows trade main-lobe width for lower side lobes
misconceptions.evidence: At N = 1024 a 1000 Hz tone gives one clean line and a 1004 Hz tone spreads out; 20 bins from the peak the level is about -36 dB with the rectangular window and about -95 dB with Blackman

misconceptions.misconception: A longer FFT always gives a better picture of the signal
misconceptions.correction: A longer frame gives finer bins but averages over more time, so a changing signal smears
misconceptions.evidence: The chirp reads about 0.9 at N = 256 but only about 0.13 at N = 4096, where its frequency rises 486 Hz during one frame

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A spectrum analyzer. The upper plot shows one frame of the input signal before and after the window function. The lower plot shows its FFT spectrum with peak markers, and optionally a scrolling spectrogram. Choose a source, FFT size, window and display below the plots and press Run to let time advance.

controls.label: Source
controls.description: Chooses a generated test signal (fs = 8000 Hz) or the microphone

controls.label: Run / Pause
controls.description: Lets time advance (the MicroSim starts paused); with the microphone source the first Run opens the microphone

controls.label: Signal frequency f
controls.description: Sets the frequency of the generated tone; disabled for the chirp and the microphone

controls.label: FFT size N
controls.description: Number of samples in each frame and in the FFT

controls.label: Window
controls.description: Window function applied to the frame before the FFT

controls.label: Display
controls.description: Shows the spectrum as linear amplitude, amplitude in dB or phase

controls.label: Spectrogram
controls.description: Adds a scrolling spectrogram (last 5 s, -80 dB to 0 dB) below the spectrum

visualElements.description: Time plot: the frame x[n] (grey) and the windowed frame x[n]w[n] (blue) against time in ms
Spectrum plot from 0 to fs/2 (8 kHz for the microphone) in linear amplitude, dB or phase, with orange peak markers and a mouse cursor
Scrolling spectrogram with a viridis colour scale from -80 dB to 0 dB
Banner with N, fs, bin spacing and frame length (or the microphone status), and a readout of the strongest peak or the bin under the cursor

model.description: Each frame of N samples is multiplied by a window and transformed with an in-place radix-2 decimation-in-time FFT. The amplitude is scaled so that a bin-centred sine reads its own amplitude; peak frequencies are refined by a parabola through the dB values of three bins.
equations: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] w[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}
Delta f = fs / N, frame length = N / fs
bin-centred sine of amplitude A: |X[k]| = A N / 2 (rectangular window)
Hanning: w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi n / N); Hamming: w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 cos(2 pi n / N)
Blackman: w[n] = 0.42 - 0.5 cos(2 pi n / N) + 0.08 cos(4 pi n / N); Kaiser: beta = 8.6
algorithms: Parabolic peak interpolation on dB values
assumptions: Generated signals are sampled at 8000 Hz; square and sawtooth waves are built from their harmonics below 4000 Hz
The microphone is read through p5.sound 0.4.1 (p5.AudioIn) at the sound card's sampling rate, with echo cancellation and noise suppression off, and is not played back
limitations: Peak frequencies from the parabolic fit are approximate
The microphone frame lags the live sound by up to about 0.2 s

instructionalStrategies: Measure known test signals first, then apply the same analyzer to live audio
Predict the bin, the raw |X[k]| and the amplitude before reading them
Compare windows at a tone placed half-way between two bins
extensions: Add zero padding to show that it interpolates the spectrum without improving resolution
